content: In resource-limited settings, while it is important to develop policies for access to third-line antiretroviral therapy (ART), this should not come at the expense of ensuring access to firstand second-line ART. For individuals whose first-line non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NNRTI)-based regimen and second-line dolutegravir (DTG)-based ART have failed, protease inhibitor (PI)-based ART may be considered as a third-line option. The choice of PI (e.g., atazanavir/ritonavir [ATV/r], darunavir/ritonavir [DRV/r], or lopinavir/ritonavir [LPV/r]) should be guided by factors such as cost, availability, and convenience. Where feasible, genotyping can be performed to optimize third-line regimen selection, including the nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NRTI) backbone. There is limited research on the use of newer antiretroviral (ARV) drugs in third-line regimens for children, adolescents, and pregnant or breastfeeding women. Pharmacokinetic and safety data for these populations are particularly scarce. Consequently, strategies must carefully balance the benefits and risks when second-line ART fails. Based on available evidence, DRV and DTG are recommended for third-line regimens in children, though there is uncertainty about whether these drugs should be used in combination or as part of a standard NRTI-based regimen. DRV cannot be used in children under three years of age and is only available in select countries through donation programs. Raltegravir (RAL) may be considered as an alternative for children who cannot use DTG and have failed PI-based second-line ART. For children with no new ARV options after second-line failure, continuing a tolerated regimen is recommended, similar to adults. If ART is discontinued, care should focus on preventing opportunistic infections, symptom relief, and pain management. There is also limited data on the use of newer third-line drugs in pregnant or breastfeeding women. Research is urgently needed to guide third-line ART strategies in resource-limited settings. Priorities include monitoring critical outcomes for individuals on second-line ART, developing heat-stable formulations of DRV/r, and evaluating the pharmacokinetics, safety, and efficacy of newer drugs in children, adolescents, and pregnant women. For treatment monitoring, viral load testing is the preferred approach to diagnose and confirm treatment failure. Point-of-care viral load testing may be used to monitor treatment among people living with HIV on ART. Routine viral load monitoring should be conducted at six months, 12 months, and then annually if the individual is stable on ART. CD4 cell count monitoring can be discontinued in settings where routine viral load testing is available for individuals established on ART. In settings without routine viral load testing, CD4 count and clinical monitoring should be used to diagnose treatment failure. Dried blood spot specimens can be used to determine HIV viral load when logistical or operational barriers prevent plasma-based testing. For individuals with a viral load above 1,000 copies/mL, enhanced adherence counseling should be provided, and viral load testing should be repeated after three months. If the viral load remains elevated, switching to an appropriate regimen is recommended. For those on NNRTI-based regimens, switching after a single elevated viral load result may be considered due to the high prevalence of NNRTI resistance in lowand middle-income countries. However, immediate switching is not recommended for individuals on DTGor PI-based regimens, as the likelihood of drug resistance is minimal. Viral load testing provides an earlier and more accurate indication of treatment failure compared to clinical or immunological monitoring, reducing the accumulation of drug resistance mutations and improving clinical outcomes. It also helps distinguish between treatment failure and non-adherence, allowing for targeted adherence support. Clinical, immunological, and virological criteria are used to define treatment failure. For adults and adolescents, clinical failure is indicated by new or recurrent severe immunodeficiency-related events after six months of effective treatment. Immunological failure is defined as a CD4 count below 250 cells/mm³ following clinical failure or persistent CD4 counts below 100 cells/mm³. For children, virological suppression may take longer than in adults. Data from studies suggest that infants and children may achieve viral suppression at a slower rate, particularly those with high baseline viral loads. Early detection of treatment failure due to pre-treatment drug resistance is beneficial, especially for individuals on NNRTI-based regimens. However, balancing this with the risk of overestimating treatment failure and unnecessary therapy switches is essential. Switching ART regimens after a single elevated viral load result is cost-effective and reduces HIV transmission and mortality, particularly for individuals with drug resistance. Enhanced adherence counseling should be emphasized during ART initiation and throughout treatment. Immediate ART switching after a single elevated viral load result should not be considered for individuals on DTGor PI-based regimens due to the low likelihood of drug resistance. Further research is needed to evaluate the clinical relevance of low-level viremia (viral load between 50 and 1,000 copies/mL) for individuals on DTGor PI-based regimens. Studies have shown that low-level viremia is associated with the development of drug resistance mutations, particularly in individuals on NNRTIor PI-based regimens. However, the clinical significance of low-level viremia for individuals on DTG-based regimens remains unclear. In summary, treatment monitoring and timely interventions are critical to optimizing ART outcomes, minimizing drug resistance, and reducing HIV transmission. Enhanced adherence support and rapid clinical action are essential, particularly for individuals on NNRTI-based regimens. Further research is needed to address gaps in knowledge, particularly for children, adolescents, and pregnant or breastfeeding women.
